summary: Sodium chloride injection is a sterile crystalloid source of sodium and chloride ions for intravenous fluid and electrolyte replacement. The 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection USP is isotonic (154 mEq/L each of Na+ and Cl-, about 308 mOsmol/L) and serves both as a fluid/electrolyte replenisher and as a vehicle or diluent for compatible IV drugs. Concentrated additive forms (e.g., 14.6% = 2.5 mEq/mL, and 23.4%) are hypertonic and MUST be diluted before administration - they are used to restore sodium in patients with restricted oral intake, specifically for hyponatremia or low-salt syndrome. Inadvertent infusion of undiluted concentrated solution can cause sudden hypernatremia with cardiovascular shock, CNS injury, hemolysis, renal cortical necrosis, and severe tissue necrosis on extravasation. Sodium is the principal extracellular cation governing water distribution, fluid balance, and osmotic pressure; both ions are regulated by the kidney.
indications: Source of water and electrolytes / fluid and electrolyte replenishment (0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection USP, isotonic)

moa: Sodium chloride in water dissociates into sodium (Na+) and chloride (Cl-) ions, normal constituents of body fluid (principally extracellular) that are essential for electrolyte balance. Sodium is the principal cation of extracellular fluid (about 90% of cations at a normal plasma concentration of ~142 mEq/L) and controls water distribution, fluid balance, and osmotic pressure; it also works with chloride and bicarbonate in acid-base regulation. When serum sodium is low, antidiuretic hormone secretion is inhibited (limiting water reabsorption) while aldosterone increases renal tubular sodium reabsorption to restore normal levels. Chloride participates in buffering during gas exchange in red blood cells. Distribution and excretion of both ions are controlled largely by the kidney.

absolute: Administration of concentrated (hypertonic) sodium chloride solutions without prior dilution
relative: Clinical states with edema and sodium retention
Cirrhosis of the liver and other sodium-retaining states
monitor: Fluid balance and signs of overhydration or pulmonary edema
Acid-base balance during prolonged parenteral therapy
Renal function, especially in the elderly and renally impaired

preg: Former Pregnancy Category C. Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted with sodium chloride; it is not known whether it can cause fetal harm or affect reproductive capacity when given to a pregnant woman. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
lact: Sodium and chloride are normal physiologic constituents, so appropriate IV replacement is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding. Caution should be exercised when administering sodium chloride to a nursing woman.
renal: Sodium chloride is substantially excreted by the kidney. Use sodium-containing solutions with great care, if at all, in severe renal insufficiency, because diminished renal function can lead to sodium retention and fluid/solute overload. Concentrated and prolonged parenteral use also carries an aluminum-toxicity risk in renal impairment. Monitor electrolytes, fluid balance, and renal function; the elderly are more likely to have decreased renal function, so use cautious dosing.
hepatic: Use sodium-containing solutions with special caution in cirrhosis of the liver and other edematous or sodium-retaining states, where sodium and fluid retention can worsen the clinical picture. Monitor fluid balance and electrolytes.

major: Corticosteroids or corticotropin (increased risk of sodium and fluid retention with sodium-containing solutions - administer with caution)
moderate: Other sodium-retaining or edema-promoting therapies (additive volume/sodium overload)
Concomitant additives that may be physically/chemically incompatible - consult a pharmacist
interactions.diagnostics: Excessive administration can dilute other serum electrolytes or cause hypernatremia; excessive potassium-free solution can produce significant hypokalemia. Monitor serum electrolytes, acid-base status, and fluid balance during therapy.

common: Reactions are largely related to excess administration or technique rather than the drug itself
serious: Hypernatremia from excess or undiluted concentrated solution
Fluid and/or solute overload with overhydration, congested states, or pulmonary edema
Dilution of other serum electrolyte concentrations
Aluminum toxicity (CNS and bone) with prolonged parenteral use in renal impairment or premature neonates
rare: Severe local tissue necrosis on extravasation of concentrated solution
Extensive hemolysis and renal cortical necrosis from inadvertent concentrated/undiluted exposure
emergency: Sudden hypernatremia with cardiovascular shock and central nervous system injury from direct injection or absorption of undiluted concentrated sodium chloride
Acute pulmonary edema / circulatory overload from large-volume infusion
Osmotic demyelination syndrome from overly rapid correction of hyponatremia

monitoring: Serum sodium and other electrolytes (especially during sodium correction)
Fluid balance, body weight, and signs of overhydration or pulmonary edema
Acid-base balance during prolonged parenteral therapy
Renal function, particularly in elderly and renally impaired patients
Neurologic status and rate of sodium change when treating symptomatic hyponatremia

Not applicable; sodium and chloride handled by renal regulation of intake and output
Depends on infused volume, renal handling, and ongoing losses

pearls: 0.9% NaCl is isotonic (~308 mOsmol/L; Na+ and Cl- 154 mEq/L each) and is the workhorse IV crystalloid and drug diluent
Concentrated forms (14.6% = 2.5 mEq/mL, 23.4%) are CONCENTRATES - must be diluted before IV use; the label warns inadvertent undiluted use can be fatal
Specific labeled niche for concentrated additive: restoring sodium in restricted oral intake, hyponatremia, or low-salt syndrome
Correct hyponatremia gradually - rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination syndrome
Aluminum-toxicity warning: prolonged parenteral use in renal impairment or premature neonates can accumulate toxic aluminum levels
0.9% sodium chloride also exists as an irrigation/wash solution (labeled NOT FOR INJECTION) - a distinct product from the IV injection forms
missed: Not applicable. Sodium chloride injection is administered and titrated by clinicians as part of fluid/electrolyte therapy rather than on a fixed self-administered schedule.
overdose: Excess administration can cause hypernatremia, fluid and solute overload (overhydration, congested states, pulmonary or peripheral edema), and dilution of other electrolytes; excessive potassium-free solution can cause hypokalemia. In the event of overhydration or solute overload, re-evaluate the patient and institute appropriate corrective measures - discontinue the infusion, correct electrolyte imbalances, and monitor fluid balance and electrolyte concentrations.
